questions.q: What is contamination in the context of evaluation design?
options: Test data or solutions leaking into training data, so a model can score well through memorization rather than genuine capability
An evaluation being run on outdated hardware
A benchmark becoming too difficult for any model to pass
A model refusing to answer evaluation questions
questions.explain: Contamination inflates scores because the model has effectively seen the answer during training, which looks like capability but isn't.

questions.q: What does prompt sensitivity reveal about an evaluation result?
options: That a result can flip substantially based on wording or framing alone, even when the underlying capability hasn't changed
That the evaluation is contaminated
That the evaluation has reached saturation
That the model's underlying capability has genuinely changed between prompts
questions.explain: Prompt sensitivity means the measured outcome depends heavily on phrasing, which is why a single prompt's result is a weak basis for a safety or capability conclusion on its own.

questions.q: What does it mean for a benchmark to be 'saturated'?
options: It has been formally retired by its creators
It only applies to safety evaluations, never capability evaluations
Scores have compressed near the ceiling across frontier models, so the benchmark no longer discriminates between them
It has become more informative over time as models improve
questions.explain: Saturation means nearly every model worth testing scores near the top, so the benchmark stops providing a useful signal about relative capability or remaining risk.

questions.q: Why is weak construct validity considered the hardest of the four pitfalls to fix?
options: Because it can be fixed simply by collecting more data
Because it only affects evaluations that are already contaminated
Because construct validity is not a real concern in AI evaluation research
Because it requires re-examining what the evaluation is actually supposed to measure, not just improving methodology or sample size
questions.explain: A benchmark can have clean methodology and still measure the wrong underlying thing, such as fluency instead of genuine persuasive effect — a problem that requires rethinking the evaluation's design, not just gathering more results.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say these four pitfalls 'compound'?
options: Because a benchmark can suffer from multiple pitfalls at once, such as being both contaminated and low in construct validity, producing a confident but completely wrong signal
Because pitfalls only apply to capability evaluations, never safety evaluations
Because only one pitfall can occur in any given evaluation
Because compounding pitfalls always cancel each other out
questions.explain: Multiple pitfalls can combine, and a benchmark that is both contaminated and poorly aligned with what it claims to measure can look highly reliable while being badly wrong.
